time/duration#

Exact immutable durations with nanosecond resolution.

Version: v1.0.0

Synopsis#

Duration(seconds: 30.rat());              // 30 seconds
Duration(seconds: (5 * 60).rat());        // 5 minutes
Duration(seconds: (2 * 3600).rat());      // 2 hours
Duration(seconds: (7 * 86400).rat());     // 7 days of 86,400 seconds
Duration(seconds: rat(250, 1000));        // 250 milliseconds
Duration(seconds: rat(1, 1000000000));    // 1 nanosecond

Description#

Exact immutable durations with nanosecond resolution.

import "io/stdout" take Stdout;
let delay = Duration(seconds: rat(3, 2));
let timeout = Duration(seconds: (5 * 60).rat());
Stdout().writeln(delay.nanoseconds().string());
Stdout().writeln(DurationString(origin: delay).string());
Stdout().writeln(DurationString(origin: timeout + delay).string());
1500000000
3/2s
603/2s

A Duration has one constructor, Duration(seconds is rat): the exact length in seconds. Other units are arithmetic at the call site, and the value is never rounded:

The seconds must come to a whole number of nanoseconds; rat(1, 3) or anything finer than a nanosecond is InvalidDuration, and so is scaling that leaves the nanosecond grid. A day here is exactly 86,400 seconds, not a civil-calendar day. Negative and zero durations are valid.

DurationString is a lossless canonical <rat>s representation. Primitive numbers deliberately have no .duration() or unit conversion methods: a stdlib type is always introduced through its explicit constructor.
